TrendTrace — 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
    Click anywhere on Earth. See what is changing, where, by how much, and whether it is statistically significant.
    
    TrendTrace is an interactive 3D globe backed by NASA Earth science missions and reanalysis/model records since 1980, requiring zero backend server.
    Clicking any location snaps to a 1° cell and computes Sen's slope per decade, a 95% confidence interval, an autocorrelation-corrected Mann–Kendall  
    p-value (Hamed–Rao, 3 lags), and a prewhitened Yue–Wang sensitivity check in the browser (~0.3 ms).                                                 
    
    Ten focus regions offer long-term series and 20 global seasonal anomaly timelapses across four metrics: GPCP v3.3 rainfall, MERRA-2 2 m temperature,
    MERRA-2 aerosol haze, and GLDAS v2.1 soil moisture. An El Niño atlas pairs 921 NOAA RONI seasons (1950–2026), 574 monthly ERSST v6 SST anomaly      
    frames, a 12-month normal-year climatology, and six detrended ENSO composite impact maps with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR hatching (q = 0.10).           
                                                                                                                                                        
    Method check: our pipeline aggregation was validated against NASA Giovanni reference series. Evaluators can click the "Present" button on the live
    site for a guided interactive walkthrough alongside our 7-slide deck
details:
WHAT TRENDTRACE IS

Built for 2026 NASA Space Apps: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!, TrendTrace is a 3D globe backed by static climate archives (zero server

required). Select NASA Earth-science mission and model variables, visualize change over time, and see what is changing, where, by how much, and

whether it is statistically significant. Click any point or region for its seasonal series, decadal trend, uncertainty, and provenance across five

seasons (ANN, DJF, MAM, JJA, SON) and four metrics: Rainfall (GPCP v3.3, mm/day, 1983–2025), 2 m Temperature (MERRA-2 reanalysis, °C, 1980–2026),

Aerosols (MERRA-2 TOTEXTTAU, 550 nm AOD, 1980–2026), and Topsoil moisture (GLDAS Noah v2.1 model, kg/m², 2000–2026), plus 20 global anomaly

timelapses. Evaluators can click the Present button on the live site (?present=1) for a guided interactive demo alongside our 7-slide deck. Source

code: https://github.com/singhg349-wq/earth-trend-detective

HOW WE DECIDE WHETHER A TREND IS REAL

A short noisy line on a chart proves nothing on its own. Every full-period record shows Sen's slope per decade, a 95% interval, a 3-lag Hamed–Rao

autocorrelation-corrected Mann–Kendall p-value, and a classic Yue–Wang prewhitening sensitivity check in plain language. Every chart defines p-value

as how unusual a trend this large would be if there were no real trend. Global trend overlays hatch false-discovery-rate significant cells at

Benjamini–Hochberg q = 0.10. Sub-period slices (Custom Year Range) display descriptive Sen slopes and means only, withholding p-values to prevent

sub-period p-hacking.

EL NIÑO HISTORY & COMPOSITE ASSOCIATIONS (NO FORECASTING)

TrendTrace includes no weather or ENSO forecasts. Instead, its El Niño page walks through 921 overlapping three-month NOAA Relative Oceanic Niño

Index (RONI) seasons (1950–2026, 44 qualifying episodes; peak RONI +2.40 °C in 1982–83, +2.28 °C in 1997–98, +2.25 °C in 2015–16), 574 monthly ERSST

v6 sea-surface temperature anomaly rasters (1979–2026), a 12-month 1991–2020 absolute temperature normal year, and six linear-detrended El Niño

minus La Niña winter composite maps (associated with, not caused by) verified by 2,000 permutations and Benjamini–Hochberg FDR (precip_DJF, t2m_DJF,

aod_SON, precip_JJA, t2m_JJA, sm_DJF).

METHOD CHECK & SCIENTIFIC LIMITS

We validated our aggregation and trend-testing pipeline against NASA Giovanni reference series and verified 26/26 Python-vs-browser statistical

parity tests; individual series export as CSV/JSON. For MERRA-2 aerosols, MODIS assimilation began c. 2000 (earlier land AOD is largely

model-driven). For soil moisture, we audited 2000–2014 GLDAS v2.0 vs v2.1 (+0.469 kg/m² jump, 3.75 kg/m² RMSE) and withheld v2.0. Live site:

https://trendtrace.earth-trend-detective-frontend.workers.dev (zero agency endorsement implied).
projectRefs: NOAA CPC Oceanic Nino Index (ONI / RONI)
